speechtext: Before the Orders of the Day are called, I would like to inquire of the Minister of Agriculture when he purposes bringing down his estimates. I may say that there is a general complaint on this side of the House among those representing agricultural constituencies, that for the last two or three sessions these estimates have been left over until a very late period in the session, and last year they were brought in on Friday night when most of the members were out of the House. This is one of the most important departments in the interest of agriculture, and I think it very unfair that these estimates should be left over to be rushed through at the latter end of the session, without giving an opportunity to discuss them pronerly.

I shall be most happy to give my hon. friend and his friends every opportunity they desire to discuss these estimates. I have not brought them down earlier, because the Experimental Farm report was only laid on the table a wreek ago, and I wished to give hon. gentlemen opposite time to consider it before taking up the estimates.

AYLESWORTH (Minister of Justice) moved that an amendment made by the Senate to Bill (No. 31), to prevent the payment or acceptance of illicit or secret commissions and other like practices, be now read the second time and concurred in. He said:	The amendment which has
been made by the Senate will be found printed in the Votes and Proceedings for the 1st of April, at page 518. It consists simply in adding to the Bill a sub-paragraph. The

Bill as it passed this House consisted of a provision that every one was guilty of an offence and liable, upon conviction, to certain penalties who being an agent, did certain things, to which the Senate has added this paragraph:
Every person who is a party, or knowingly privy, to any offence under this Act shall he guilty of such offence, and shall be liable, upon conviction, to the punishment hereinbefore provided for by this section.
The general law, under a provision of the Criminal Code, is that every accessorv before the fact is guilty as a principal. This amendment irossibly goes a little further; that is a matter upon which I would hesitate to express any definite opinion. But if it does go any further than the general law, it is in a direction which I think will meet the approval of the House. It is simply nroviding that any person who is party or knowingly privy to the offence or offences which this Bill prohibits, shall be deemed to be equally guilty with the principal offender. I thought that there could be no objection to that clause being added to the Bill, and therefore I move the second reading.
Motion agreed to.

On section 1,

["Before this resolution passes, I think this would be an opportune time to bring to the notice of the hon. minister and the government the great necessity which exists for a port of call in Nova Scotia for those lines in the summer time. Take this proposed line of steamers which ply between Montreal and Quebec and some port in France, we are told by the hon. minister that fish, particularly lobsters, is one of our largest exports to France. It would therefore be a great boon to Cape Breton and the coast of Nova Scotia if we had a port somewhere in the Province to which these steamers would call and on which we could ship our fish and other exports to France, where there' is an excellent market for them. These steamers will pass by our doors practically within a few miles, and it will be too bad if provision be not made for them to call at North Sydney. At that port there is considerable French trade. It is the headquarters of the French trawlers, a trade which has only been developed the last few years. These steamers also take a large quantity of coal, and it would be much cheaper for them to purchase it at North Sydney rather than at Montreal or Quebec. If they were to call at North Sydney, they would there get their bunker much more expeditiously and cheaply, which would be an inducement to them to call there. What I have said regarding this new line between Canada and France also applies to the steamers plying between Canada and Mexico. In the maritime provinces, we have no chance of communicating with those lines unless they call somewhere on the coast of Nova Scotia, and North Sydney is 'the nearest point and not at all out of their way. The English mail has been landed there, and if that does not put the mail steamers much out of their course, the delay would be still less of a disadvantage in the case of freight boats. Besides North Sydney being the terminus of the Intercolonial Railway, it u'ould become the point of shipping for the whole province of Nova Scotia and the provinces of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island during the summer thus giving to those provinces the advantage of the French market. The existing law provides that municipal councils may lease certain wharfs. It is proposed to give to the Governor in Council the right to lease wharfs to shipping and railway companies also. This Bill is framed on the same lines as the legislation now existing with regard to piers and breakwaters under the control of the Department of Public Works.
What control does the government keep over the rates to be charged on wharfs so leased?

The rates will be the same as they are to-day in the case of wharfs leased to municipal councils. The main object of the Bill is to enable the department to commute the tolls in order to avoid the great difficulty of collection. We have a number of wharfs leased in this way to the Richelieu and Ontario Company, although I do not know that the leases are strictly legal; the arrangement is giving great satisfaction and I think we receive more revenue than from similar wharfs that are not leased.

Does the minister not think that this might lead to great injustice to some shipping companies which would be placed at the mercy of their competitors? Charges of that kind were made with reference to the Standard Oil Com-

pany in its dealings with other companies upon railroads owned by it. Is there any tribunal to which these rates may be submitted from time to time?
We intend to take that power by the leases which will be granted under this Act.
Why not put it in the Act? If by accident, for instance, it should be omitted from the lease it would be most unfair.
Care will of course be taken that that provision is put in the lease.
What increased powers are given in this Act over the powers given in the Act of 1906?
There is no change in the first section from the Act of 1906, except that power is given to lease not only to municipal councils and provincial governments but also to shipping and railway companies.

I would make the following suggestions to the minister: That the wharfs or piers should be leased after public tender; that the leases should be given for a limited number of years and that the government should fix the tolls to be charged before calling for tenders. If the leases fell in after a number of years it might be possible to obtain a much higher rental for the second term owing to the development of business. I am not making these suggestions in any spirit of hostile criticism, as I think it is perhaps better to have the government lease a wharf than to maintain a staff and receive little or no revenue.

Our object is to secure a larger revenue. My hon. friend is probably aware that we have many wharfs from which we derive practically no revenue. It is a matter of great difficulty to get any revenue at all from these wharfs under the present system by which the consignees of the goods are charged five cents, or ten cents, or fifteen cents, a package, and it often costs more to collect it, if you can collect it at all, than the debt is worth. The idea is to average the business done at each whaTf during the past few years, and after having ascertained the amount of business done by each steamboat company using the wharf, to fix a Tental for its use on that basis. I believe in this way we will get a revenue from these wharfs which it is impossible for us to get under the present arrangement. In the case of several wharfs in the lower St. Lawrence the Richelieu and Ontario Navigation Company has been authorized by order in council to commute the Tates and the object of this Bill is to legalize that system and to ex-Mr. SPROULE.
tend it. Under the Bill we take the power to lease the wharfs as is done in the Public Works Department, and we also take power to commute the rates. Possibly the steamship companies may add the wharfage dues to the freight rates but whether or not the system will be more convenient to the public and to the department. My hon. friend (Mr. J. A. Currie) has suggested that we should lease these wharfs by tender and that might be a satisfactory system if there were several persons or companies who were competing for the same wharf, but in the great majority of cases I think only one company uses the wharf.

The charges on these wharfs are paid by the shippers and not by the carrying company, and there is nothing in the Bill which says that the tolls shall be fixed by the government. Neither is there anything in the Bill to prevent the lessee of the wharf excluding the general public or other steamship companies from the use of that wharf.
It is not the intention to create a monoply.

It is well known that in many cases the steamship companies have wharfs of their own which they will not allow the public to use except on the payment of fees, so that the only relief outside steamers have is to tie up at the government wharf and discharge their cargo. Before this Bill is passed there should be provision made to take care that the public shall have the free use of government wharfs. It is quite true that a number of government wharfs do not pay any revenue, but it is also true that the only place certain steamers have to land their cargo is at the government wharfs as distinguished from privately owned wharfs.

In any case, where more than one company would wish to use a government wharf, it would of course be stipulated as a condition of the lease that others should have the right to its use. It is not the intention to create a monopoly at all. As to the leasing of the wharfs I do not know whether we will take a great deal of advantage of this legislation or not, because, so far, I do not think there are four wharfs leased to municipal councils. I do not know whether there aTe two even. I know of one only. Perhaps there has been another one leased during the past year. But, so far, the provision has not been taken advantage of. So, it was thought that if we had the same legislation as they have in the Public Works Department, under the Public Works Act, we might induce some railway and shipping companies to take advantage of it. The part of the Bill to which we attach the greatest importance

is that which makes provision for a commutation of rates for a certain sum of money so as to avoid the necessity of undertaking do collect small sums of money from different individuals, an undertaking which is not always successful. I am under the impression that the Act will be taken advantage of by companies which may use those wharfs. We will make arrangements with three or four companies for the use of a wharf according to the volume of business they are doing at that wharf. There will be no monopoly. It will be an advantage to us not to have to collect these wharfage rates but to charge these companies a lump sum for the use of the wharfs.

I would like to draw the minister's attention to (the fact that in the building of some of these wharfs the government have monopolized the only approaches to them so that the general public have no method of getting into the towns and villages in which these wharfs are situated except over the property that the government have taken advantage of in the building of the wharfs. Consequently, any man coming to town to buy a few groceries or a bag of flour can only get his goods into his boat or conveyance over the property that the government have taken possession of. If this property is handed over to some steamboat company which would naturally like to cut out that means of transportation they could very easily prevent people from getting in or out of town by charging a toll which would be exorbitant. I think that in handling this matter the government ought to protect the people who would be affected in this way. There is only wharf accommodation to a limited extent and they should not be subjected to a toll in getting in or out of town with a small boat such as I have referred to. In many of these places there are little boats and tugs that are perhaps not controlled by any one particular company, and I do not think the full control of these wharfs should be handed over to any steamboat company. It would be in the interest of the government and of the public if these small wharfs-I am referring now more particularly to the small wharfs-were handed over to the municipal councils. You are taking the power to do that but at the same time you are taking the power to hand them over to steamboat companies.

This provision has been in the law for many years but unfortunately it has not been taken advantage of by the municipal councils. I am informed there are two municipal councils which have taken advantage of it. This law has been in existence since 1886.

I would draw the minister's attention to the fact that the Department of Public Works has only handed over a few of the wharfs to his deoartment. Consequently there has been no opportunity for the municipal councils to assume control of these wharfs. In the riding which I represent three wharfs have been built, two in rather an important place and in the important places the Department of Public Works has kept control of them. Nobody is in charge of them, and everybody is using them as he likes. One of the unimportant wharfs has been handed over to the minister's department, a wharfinger has been appointed and he is exercising his sweet will and charging the general public whatever he likes to go over this wharf. There should be some control in a matter of this kind.

Unfortunately, that legislation by which municipal councils can get possession of wharfs has been in existence for many years and no advantage has been taken of it except in two cases. It is probably because municipal councils are afraid of some burden being put upon them for keeping up these wharfs. If they took over these wharfs they would have to make some ordinary repairs to them. We propose to extend the provision to shipping and railway companies which would take advantage of it because they are more interested than the municipal councils. I do not know what effect it may have but it is in order to obtain a better administration of the wharfs than we have to-day that we are taking this step. As I said a few moments ago the main object is to get a commutation of rates so that we may charge the shipping companies who are using these wharfs a certain fixed sum of money instead of being obliged to collect the small wharf rates that are very difficult to collect. There are several wharfs which have been transferred to this department. It is proposed, after this legislation is passed, that all these wharfs shall be transferred and that active steps shall be taken to secure the good and proper administration of them.

I would like to ask the minister how it happens that the policy of the department is to get rid of these wharfs by leasing them to private individuals, corporations and councils on the one hand while on the other he is buying up wharfs, as for instance, at Oshawa, Bowmanville, Whitby and other places After buying these wharfs with the object of getting friends of the government out of a hole they are going to turn around and lease them to somebody else. Another point is that in many places, especially along the rivers and inland lakes, the wharf occupies the only available site in the town. It is the intention of the gov' eminent to lease a wharf that costs a few

hundred or a few thousand dollars, to some individual and allow him to charge rates for traffic with the creation of which he had absolutely nothing to do? My hon. friend from Muskoka (Mr. Wright) has referred to the wharf at Bracebridge which occupies the only available point along the shore of the river. .
That is a private wharf.
The government assisted in building it. It was promised by the former Postmaster General as an election bribe some years ago.

speechtext: Order.
Not at all; I want no order about it. He told the electors that if they returned a certain man they would assist them in the building of that wharf.

speechtext: He is a judge wf the land now and that makes it all the worse.

speechtext: Order, order.

I want the minister to look into this matter and, where wharfs are being let, to take particular pains to see that no monopoly shall be given to the man who occupies the wharf which is in the only possible place where a wharf can be located in the town.

I think there is the possibility of grave abuses growing up under this system. I can understand why there are not very many of these wharfs rented by municipalities as the governmnt could desire. One reason is because they do not want to assume the responsibility for the damages in the event of injury. A portion may be swept away or other damages may be done for which they may be liable, and that is one reason they do not want it. Another reason is that it must be kept safe for use. That implies responsibility, the extent of which may be unknown, and therefore they are reluctant to assume it. But what seems to me of more interest is this. The minister speaks always of these corporations and wants to commute the rates and receive so much iin a lump sum in return for the use of the wharf, and the lessees will have the right to fix the rates on every ton of freight that passes over the whaFf- The individual gets a lease of that wharf at a given lump sum per year and then will charge as much as he can to the public for the use of it. If the government do not keep control over the rates and have the power to reduce them from time to time injustice will be done the public.

Another objection is the length of time for which a wharf may be rented. In the ease oif some towns, a wharf is of very little importance in early history, and might be leased for a very small figure, just as the water-power of the Cornwall canal was leased for 84 years; but as the town developed, the amount of freight passing over that wharf may increase very considerably and the lease be a very profitable speculation. Again, where one line sends large quantities over the wharf, it may be allowed a lower rate than the ordinary public who ship small quantities. Unless there be some safeguard in the Act itself to prevent the possibility of such abuses, the public may seriously suffer. Take for instance the case of the town of Thornbury, in connection with which I had something to do with getting the Act passed. They had to submit their schedule of rates to the inspection of the department. If it was reasonable, the department ratified it, but the municipality which had control could not make a charge until the rate was consented to by the government.

It will be provided that the rates must be approved by order in council. You must not mix up the two things, the leasing of wharfs and the commutation of rates. In the first instance, if there be several companies,the wharf will not be leased, as that will not be necessary, but it would be in the interest of the revenue that we should say to the companies : ' You will pay us each a certain amount for the use of the wharf.' We will then not be obliged, as we are to-day, to collect those small amounts which it is almost impossible to collect.

Suppose a lumber company owns the wharf and the government commutes the rates, and the lumber company bring in their own lumber free over that wharf, the public may be obliged to pay 50 cents a 1,000 feet for any lumber they bring over it.
They will not be in that position because we will know exactly the business they are doing before we lease the wharf, and under the law we can only lease it for a term of three years.
Who will keep the docks in repair, and what control will the government retain?
The company which leases the wharf will make the ordinary repairs.
Will the government have an inspector to see that the docks are kept in proper repair.

My idea is to have a
wharfinger who will look after the docks

and will report on the way the business is carried on.
Why not have a provision in the lease requiring the lessee to keep the dock in repair subject to the inspection of the government?
That is a good suggestion.

This is rather dangerous legislation. Looking over the total revenue from the wharfs of this country and comparing them with the enormous amount expended on these wharfs since this government has been in power, it seems to me that a considerable amount of carelessness is chargeable to some department. The minister has stated, this afternoon, as he has frequently done on the estimates, that there is no revenue from certain wharfs because they have not been handed over by the Public Works Department to his department. There are cases where the Public Works Department has expended large amounts on wharfs which have not been handed over to the Marine and Fisheries Department, and from which there is no revenue to the country, although completed years ago. My hon. friend does not deny that. Well, if it is the nolicy of the government to spend large amounts on wharfs in the public interest, I am not going to complain, provided the money is well expended and the expenditure required in the public interest. No legislation should be passed that would allow the minister to lease these wharfs to any private individual or corporation. I believe the proper policy is for the government to own the wharf, to fix rates of toll and to appoint their own official to look after the business, thus placing everybody who wishes to use the wharf on the same looting. This Bill will allow the minister to select a friend-I am not speaking from a political standpoint-and give him the absolute power over any given wharf. It is true, the minister says the government will fix the rates. But if they fix the rates, why should not they appoint a wharfinger to collect those rates and let the money come into the public treasury? If this is not done, some one company will get control and will squeeze out other people who wish to do business at the wharf. This is already being done at some wharfs in eastern Canada that I could name. It is the public money that has been spent in these works, and the department go so far as to say that they will not expend a dollar of money upon a wharf that is not owned by the government. I would not complain of that if the government would only carry it out in every case-and I am free to say that they do not carry it out in every case. If it is the policy of the government to own these wharfs, to spend every dollar that is spent upon them in construction and repairs, why
not appoint a public official to take charge and give everybody equal opportunities ?
What case has the minister in mind in which he will be justified in leasing?
The wharfs on the St. Lawrence and great lakes especially. We have been trying to lease these wharfs to municipalities, but so far we have not found the municipalities ready to take charge of them.
And never will.

But, though the municipalities are not ready to lease these wharfs, perhaps we can find steamship companies or railway companies that will do so. And the object of this legislation is to extend the existing power to lease to municipalities so as to authorize the lease to shipping or railway companies. Since 1886, we have had legislation authorizing the lease to munici palities or provincial governments, and, except in two cases, this legislation has not been availed of. If we lease to a private company, the department will be relieved of the necessity of looking after these wharfs as closely as it does to-day. My hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) has drawn attention to the fact that we could continue the existing system

I did not ask the government to continue the existing system, because it is a very bad one; it allows the Public Works Department to keep control of wharfs for many years instead of handing them over to the Marine and Fisheries Department.

Even if handed over to the Marine and Fisheries Department, we might still be in the same position as we are in many cases to-day. In some cases we cannot get anybody to take charge of the wharfs, cannot get wharfingers, because we pay them only a percentage of the receipts.
Pay them what is right.

We have no money provided in the estimates for that purpose, and so these wharfingers are paid by fees. But the amount collected is so small in many cases and the collection involves so much difficulty that we cannot find people to take these positions. The man who occupies the position of wharfinger is obliged practically to quarrel with all the persons in the locality. He has to ask them for small sums of money, it may be ten cents or it may be as much as a dollar, and it is always a great source of trouble for him. That is why we suggest the commutation of rates with shipping and railway companies, they to pay a certain amount and to receive the right to charge the rates which are charged to-day.
Does not the statement the hon. minister has just made suggest to him that his government have been expending large amounts of money in small places where the expenditure is absolutely unnecessary?

It is not so much a question of expense, but because this is a very arduous job and it is very unpleasant for a man living in the locality to be obliged to collect these small sums from his neighbours. Many who have accepted the position of wharfinger have resigned.

I think there can be no possible objection to clause 2 of this Bill, and I think it is absolutely necessary to have such a provision. As the minister tells us, it is much easier to collect an annual rental from a steamship company or an individual desiring to use the wharf than to collect tolls on an amount of freight landed on the wharf.

Does not the hon. gentleman (Mr. A. K. Maclean) see that some person will have to deal with the public? And is he prepared to state that it would be better to have a steamship company deal with the public in an arbitrary way-

Under clause 2, the company will simply have the use of the wharf; it is not leased to them. But instead of paying a toll for each use made of the wharf they pay a fixed sum. They have no control over the wharf, and the arrangement with them does not affect the user of the wharf by other people. So I do not think there can be any possible objection to the second clause of the Bill.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. A. K. Maclean) is astray. The minister proposes to give the steamship company the exclusive right to collect tolls.
This second clause simply provides that any company or person may pay a fixed annual sum for the use of the wharf.
And he collects the toll.
It does not exclude other people from the use of the wharf.
The company collects in place of the officer who is there-now.
No.
That is the way the minister explained it.

No, they pay a fixed sum for the use of the wharf. I do not' see why there should be any opposition to this clause. There may be some Mr. BRODEUR.
cases in which it would be well for the department to have the power to lease the wharf, but still I would submit to the minister that such instances would be very few indeed, and that very great care should be exercised by the department in leasing a wharf. A word with regard to the remarks of the hon. member from Peel (Mr. Blain) as to the collection of tolls. There are many cases in which it is very difficult and a hardship to exact toll. The wharf may be erected at a place where there are but a few people, and yet the wharf may be a great necessity and may mean a great deal to the people of that place. It may be a great hardship even to exact tolls from them, and the public as a whole would be pleased to make the expenditure even though they have no hope of receiving revenue by way of tolls.
Would my hon. friend suggest how this change will improve that condition of affairs.

I am not saying that it will improve it, it would operate in the direction which my hon. friend desires. I merely wish to say that the Department of Marine and Fisheries will find many cases where it will be difficult to exact tolls, and where the public will justify the department in giving free use of the wharf to the public.
The minister says there is no change in the principle with regard to leasing wharfs; but at the same time he says there is a change with regard to the classes of persons who may use these wharfs.

The existing law is found in section 20, chapter 39 of the Revised Statutes, applied to the Department of Public Works, and which Teads as follows:
The minister may enter into arrangements with any provincial government, municipal council, or other local corporation or authority, or with any company in the provinces of Ontario or Quebec, incorporated for the purpose of constructing or holding the works mentioned in this section, or works of like nature in the same province, for the transfer to them of any of the public roads, harbours, rivers or river improvements, bridges or public buildings, whether within or without the limits of the local jurisdiction of such municipal council or other authorities, which it is found convenient to place under their management.
2. On the completion of such arrangements, the Governor in Council may grant and, by so granting, transfer and convey forever or for any term of years, all or any of such roads, harbours, rivers and river improvements, bridges or public buildings, to such provincial government, municipal council or other local authority or company, upon such terms and conditions as are agreed upon; and

the said governments, municipal councils or other local authorities may enter into such arrangements and may take and hold any works so transferred.
So here is a principle which has been embodied in our legislation for 25 or 30 years, but so far it has not been taken advantage of by the Public Works Department. As my hon. friend is aware, after a wharf is constructed it may be transferred to the Department of Marine and Fisheries to be administered. Then we have a law in our department which is to be found in the Revised Statutes, chap. 12, sec. 16, providing that we may lease these wharfs to municipal councils. In this case provincial governments are not mentioned. This legislation has never been taken advantage of except m two cases; no municipal council has been willing to lease and take charge of these wharfs. When the legislation was introduced in 1886 it was thought that municipal councils would be willing to take advantage of this legislation, but they have not done so. We are considering the policy of extending this privilege to some other persons who probably would take more interest in the administration of these wharfs, and we thought that shipping companies and railway companies might do so if we introduced into the Act the same provision that exists with regard to the Public Works Department. That is the reason why we are extending this legislation, that is why we are asking power to lease, not only to municipal councils, but also to shipping and railway companies. Perhaps they will not take advantage of it : but it may be that some public body will take advantage of this legislation if they are allowed to do so.

Now the minister has made it clear. This is not an extension of the same principle, but it is an entire alteration of the principle with Tegard to dealing with such piers and wharfs as are handed over to the Department of Marine and Fisheries. The minister will see there is a vast difference between leasing a wharf to a provincial government, thereby putting that wharf within the control of a government for the benefit of all the people, and giving the minister power to put that wharf under the jurisdiction of a steamboat. or a railway company, or a private individual. It is rather a dangerous invasion of a public right which is given under the old section, and one which I think, as the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Maclean) says, should be exercised with extreme caution. My hon. friend says he proposes to apply this to wharfs on the great lakes. I am particularly interested there. My hon. friend will see that if he applies that principle to wharfs on the great lakes 140	1 1
as he does to any other part of Canada, it would be liable to grave abuses, particularly where there are few transportation companies, and these are operating where traffic is small and where distances are great. Where possibly a transportation company may be the only Targe corporation using a wharf, the power may be open to serious abuses. Once give a steamboat or a railway corporation, or a person, any vested rights, any exclusive rights, subject to whatever conditions or restrictions the minister may see fit to impose, and he thereby excludes to some extent the rights that the general public enjoyed. For instance, let the minister give to a local steamboat company along the shores of Lake Superior, or along the rivers, the exclusive privilege by lease of a pier, and that .steamboat company will at once begin to dictate terms to the public, will begin to act in a drastic and sometimes tyrannical manner towards the public, and subject the public to serious inconveniences which may not come to the notice of the minister for a considerable time. I do not see any necessity for departing from the principle which was laid down in 1886, and which is referred to by my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain). Let these wharfs be public utilities, let the public have equal rights with respect to them; let John Jones have the same rights to a wharf as a steamboat company or a railway company, and do not let it be possible, if John Jones wishes to use that wharf for his little traffic, for him to run foul of a steamboat company, or a transportation company, or some person, whose business is served by that wharf, and be told forsooth that they have a lease in that wharf from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. It would involve a great deal of correspondence with Ottawa, from a long distance, before the matter could be set right by the minister. There is a danger in the extent of power which is granted to the minister.
Another thing occurs to me. There are appropriations for new wharfs on Lake Superior, and is it not competent, under the first part of section 16, for the Department of Public Works to make appropriations for the building of government wharfs and piers in places where they would substantially serve the interest of only one individual, or one corporation trading in the vicinity, such as a lumber firm, or a merchant carrying on extensive business in the vicinity. When a wharf is erected and paid for by the government it may then be leased to a lumber or transportation company or a private merchant, say for 20 years, at such rental and under such terms and conditions as the minister sees fit to impose so that no monopoly of that wharf may be given to the detriment of the people of the district.



I simply wish to point out the dangers of abuse under the proposed legislation.
Do we collect tolls from all government wharfs or are there some from which we collect no tolls?

There have been transferred from the Department of Public Works to the Department of Marine and Fisheries 416 wharfs and we have been collecting revenue from 224 of these. In some cases we cannot get a man to act as wharfinger as his duties may involve him in difficulties with his neighbours. That of course is generally in small places where there is little business.
How about the wharfs on the Great Lakes?
They are the best we have, we have the least trouble with them.

Where the revenue is so small that you cannot get a wharfinger, I would suggest that it would be better to make the wharf entirely free for the benefit of the people in the district. Do not let us go into this partnership business with companies and individuals in regard to the building of wharfs.
We will draw the line.

I would draw the line more strictly than the government has been drawing it in reference to the build ing of wharfs. Wharfs have been built at many places where they are not needed and I would suggest that in these places too where the revenue is only $25 or $50 a year, the wharfs should be made free. There are many of these unnecessary wharfs and whatever benefit there is to be obtained from them should go to the public and not to the middleman, the intermediary, the friend of the government. The minister speaks as if this Bill were simply enlarging the scope of section 16 of chapter 112 of the Harbours and Piers Act, extending a system that has been in vogue for many years. As a matter of fact we are adopting an entirely new principle. The original Act provides that where the annual receipts from any wharf for the three years previous have not exceeded $100 the minister may lease the wharf to the municipality within which it is situated, for a term not exceeding three years. The proposed amendment permits the Governor in Council to lease any wharf, whether the lease be $100 or $10,000 for any length of time to any company or person under any conditions they see fit to impose and they need not make any provision as to whether the public shall or shall not be accommodated or whether the tolls shall be reasonable. The government is not bound to do that, because under section 2, before the matter goes to council, Mr. BOYCH.
the minister has the alternative of entering into an agreement, in eases where there is not sufficient revenue to support a wharfinger, to divide the revenue with the company or person to whom the wharf is leased. The minister may divide that little pittance and he may say to the company: I will commute the rates with you and there shall be an amount payable yearly by you and we shall have to engage a wharfinger annually as to the balance. I am entirely opposed to anything of this kind. I am speaking of it more because there is a principle involved. If we build railways and pay for them let us control them; if we build canals and the people pay for them let the people have them; if we build a transcontinental railway and the people dip down into their pockets and provide all the funds it is unfair that the company should reap the reward. This is just a means of having a certain amount of truckery that we don't want. If the people supply the money to build these wharfs let the people have the accommodation they afford. If a wharf is not necessary do not build it, but if you do build it let it be used in the public interest and not in the interest of middlemen and hangers on, which would be the result of this legislation. This will result in a large army of people coming and pestering the ministers and members to build more wharfs. Lumber companies that have timber away back in the interior which they cannot get out will want the government to build wharfs for them.
As in the Grande Vallee case.

Grande Vallee is one of them and there are others. They will get the government to build a wharf on the understanding that as soon as it is built it shall be controlled by them for a nominal rental, and the public shall have the pleasure of paying, and the private company shall have the pleasure of getting all the benefit.

I wish to point out another danger that must occur if the government wharfs are handed over to private individuals. My riding borders on one of the great lakes and even at present while the wharfs are under the control of the government we have this difficulty:	That a
vessel is lying at a particular point in the wharf and occupying a particular space, and for reasons of their own they do not want to move her far enough in or far enough out to allow another vessel to lie at that side of the wharf where it would have protection from storms. I have seen the government wharfingers having to throw the lines off a boat and let her go adrift if they refuse to move her up or

down. If that wharf were controlled by the owners of the vessel that was lying there you could see what difficulty the owner of another vessel would have in getting his vessel to the wharf. That is a danger you have to take into account in leasing these wharfs to private individuals. Then again, a lumber company could so pile up that wharf with lumber and keep it there for storage all summer that the public would be greatly hampered in the general use of that wharf. I know something about these difficulties because I have been up against them myself, and I hope the minister will not hand the wharfs over to private individuals.

After hearing what has been said by hon. gentlemen opposite I think we should not go the length of giving private individuals the right to lease these wharfs. It would probably bring more trouble on the department than it has now, and I would be willing to strike out the provision about leasing to private individuals.
And to companies as well.

The transportation companies are in a different position because they are serving the public. On Lake Erie, the Canadian Pacific Railway has the exclusive use of a wharf and I think it should be leased to them for the special purpose they use it for. In the same way the Grand Trunk has a wharf at Parry Sound which is used by them exclusively.
You would not have to pay a wharfinger in that case at all.
Oh, yes, we will require wharfingers.
There is no provision in the Bill giving the Railway Commission or any other body supervision of the tolls which may be charged by railway companies on these wharfs.
One of the conditions of the lease would be that they should charge the rates provided by the order in council.

But under this section, as I read it, the department would have the right to build a new wharf and lease it to a steamship company or a railway company without any provision for maintaining the rights of the general public.

That is not the intention. In cases in which we have leased wharfs to the municipal councils they have been required to charge the same rates as were charged by the public wharfs under the control of the department. It is intended to continue that system.
140i	. ! i | i !

The Department of Public Works controls a certain number of wharfs and the Department of Marine and Fisheries controls others, and let me suggest that all the wharfs should be transferred to the Marine Department. Then, the Minister of Marine should make out a statement by next session of parliament of the total number of wharfs owned by the government, and if there are special ones which he wants to lease to certain companies let him bring down a Bill empowering him to do so. I fancy he has not studied those as thoroughly as he ought to have done because he now offers to withdraw a portion of it. Let him come down and place a statement of all the wharfs the government owns before the House. Then let him propose legislation dealing with a certain number that the government ought to lease to steamship and railway companies and make regulations governing the whole pf the balance as to what the rates shall be, defining those that will be under wharfingers and those that the government will allow to be used free of rates by the public. It would be better to come to a business arrangement with regard to the whole system of wharfs and introduce new legislation with regard to all the wharfs owned by the country. I think that would be a better plan than perhaps getting us into trouble by passing this legislation now when neither side of the House thoroughly understands it.

I do not think there would be any trouble, because, as far as the wharfs which are to-day under the control of the Department of Public Works are ccncerned, legislation similar to this has been in existence and has not been taken advantage of. However, in view of the suggestion which has been made by th^ hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox), and the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Boyce), I think we might make a modification in this Bill. Perhaps some abuses would be created if we were given power to lease to private persons. Lumber companies have been referred to, and perhaps these companies would like to have the power to lease these wharfs. Possibly that should not be done. I am willing that they should not have the power to lease these wharfs notwithstanding the fact that this power has been in existence under the Public Works Act and that no abuses seem to have resulted from it. But in view of the discussion which has taken place, I realize that some abuses might occur. This is an experiment in order to meet the situation which exists to-day. To-day the situation with regard to these wharfs is far from being satisfactory. We have legislation in the Department of Marino and Fisheries providing that these wharfs should be leased to municipal councils, but it has not resulted as we had ex-

peeted it would. This clause has been on the statute-book for twenty-three years and it has not been taken advantage of except in two cases. Now, we are proposing to extend this power to shipping and railway companies and also to private individuals. But, in view of the discussion which has taken place we might drop out the portion which concerns private persons and confine it to municipal councils, harbour commissioners, shipping and railway companies. I am sure that with the conditions that are put into this law there will be no abuses in so far as the public are concerned, and it will give the department a better means of administering these wharfs.

Let me tell the minister what happened in our town. We had two or three private wharfs. A railway company acquired control of them and nobody could land at the town without going over the railway property. They, of course, charged for every trunk and everything else that passed over these wharfs, and the result was that in order to satisfy the requirements of the people the town itself had to spend $2,000 or $3,000 to build a public wharf. They have that wharf now free to the citizens of the town. That might happen in a number of towns where my hon. friend would rent wharfs to shipping or railway companies. They might collect wharf rates where people have been in the habit of using the government property at lower rates or practically free. The railway and shipping companies will not allow this. 1 think it would be better for the minister to look into the whole question of the wharfs controlled by the Public Works Department and his own department, ascertain which of these wharfs can be properly leased to railway and shipping companies and then let the government lay down a tariff that they cannot exceed.
That is what is to be done.
No, this does not make provision for that.

In case of a wharf being leased it will be provided that they will not be able to charge more than the order in council allows. The company leasing the wharf will have the administration of it and they will probably relieve the department of the repairs which appertain to it.
Why would not the second clause meet the case of railway and steamship companies?

I think the clause giving power to the minister to lease to railway and shipping companies is a most dangerous clause. The public might be affected very injuriously by the power which would be conferred upon a steamboat company to charge exorbitant rates as against any other Mr. BRODEUR.
steamboat company using that wharf. I think that provision ought to be made, if you are going to lease a wharf to a steamboat company, that other companies shall have equal powers to utilize that wharf. I think there should be no charge for all small shipping as against farmers and others who may have occasion to go over a leased wharf. If there is no limitation of this kind it will shut them out from using a leased wharf when they desire to go to the town to do their shopping or attend to their business. These people have to get over the wharf some way, and the steamboat company which has a lease from the government will be able to charge them a toll which may be prohibitive. I would like to ask the minister a question with regard to the present condition of affairs. Do the wharfingers have to submit the toll charged to the minister for his approval?

Orders in council have been passed at different times giving the rates which are to be charged on these wharfs. My hon. friend speaks of the danger of a company charging exorbitant rates for the use of a wharf by other persons. There is no danger because it has always been provided in the law and it is the intention to nrovide in this law that they shall not have the right to charge anything more than the rates provided for in the order in council. Everybody will always be on the same footing.

I see very great danger in handing over the exclusive control of a wharf to any individual or steamship company. They can go up to a whaTf, transfer their goods over it and shut out every other man. Even if another company had a right to the wharf under a lease it would be almost impossible to enforce that right. I have seen these wharfs built by the government and supposed to be under the control of the Public Works Department, utilized by aisingle steamboat company to the detriment of all others. I have even seen them used for the piling of a hundred cords of wood which may be allowed to remain there for weeks and months and the people have to go around and land as best they can on the river frontage. I do not think a steamboat company should have any lease that would give them greater power than any other company or individual.	i
In a case where there is only one shipping company that goes to a wharf it would be advantageous to have it leased to that company in order that the company might look after the wharf.

In all the northern waters there are gasoline launches, canoes, row-boats, and lumbermen's boats, and craft of all kinds, which might not be described as steamboats, and which might be put in the unenviable position of being

refused landing facilities by the steamboat company in charge of the wharf.
It could not do that.

I agree to some extent with hon. gentlemen in their opinion against the policy of leasing wharfs, and I do not see why the second clause does not give the department ample power to deal with any case such as that described by the minister in connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Grand Trunk Railway. If the Governor in Council is to be given power under clause 16, there should be some amendment to that Bill in order that the public rights be more amply protected. There should be some terms and conditions defined. I suggest that the hon. minister, after the discussion we have had this afternoon, should let the Bill stand over in order that some amendment may be devised to clause 16. It is rather difficult to draft one off-hand.

I have no objection to having the Bill stand in order to see whether an amendment might not be drafted to protect the public against any possible danger. Our intention is not to give any undue privilege to anybody, but simply to obtain the power to better administer the wharfs under our control.

I would call attention to the fact that the proposition may be very serious to Manitoba. We have in Selkirk a wharf with about 2,000 feet frontage, and if it be possible to lease that to one shipping company, a dangerous monopoly might be created. Under the present arrangement, there is one company, which has a large business in lumber and fish, which practically monopolizes the wharf to-day. There is so much lumber piled on it at times, that it is almost impossible to walk down the docks. I do not know whether it has been passed over to the Marine Department or not.
I do not see it in my list.
There is the trouble. I presume it is under the control of the Public Works Department, and the public have no recourse against the inconvenience from which they are suffering.

There is no mention of it at all in the public accounts.
Mr PLAIN I presume we get no revenue from it at all. If this Bill becomes law, there are two or three companies doing a large business at this wharf arid the minister will be compelled to make a selection among them.

No, my intention is simply to provide for places where there is no competition, and where consequently no one company can be given preference to the detriment of another. In cases where there is only one company, it would be an improvement to give that company a lease under the control of the department and on the condition specified in the lease.
Would not that be creating a monopoly?
No, because there would be only one company. Where there are two or three companies, there would be no necessity to exercise the power given by that Bill.
Who controls the wharf at Selkirk? There is a wharfinger there who is paid some $300 a year. Is he paid by the government or the steamboat men?
I do not know about that. That wharf is not on my list.
There is nothing in the blue-book to indicate who pays this man.
I do not know about this wharf. I will make inquiries.

So far as the records show, there is no wharf there at all-no account of it in either the Public Works or the Marine Department. Money was voted to build a wharf there, but there i3 no revenue, no wharfinger appointed, no further record of it. It may be like the armouries in Toronto-nobody seems to know who owns them or what department holds them. The Public Works Department seems to get a certain distance with these works, and even to finish them, but without turning them over to any department to take charge of them. There is no account of any revenue from the wharf at Selkirk. I approve of the proposal of the minister to have these wharfs taken over and administered by his department. It should have been done long ago. As to the matter of tolls, in case of a lease, to prevent exorbitant rates, could not the matter be left to the Railway Commission to deal with on complaint of parties who feel aggrieved? Other things of this kind are left to the Railway Board, and perhaps this suggestion may meet with the approval of the minister.
In the case of a railway it might be done, but not in the others. These rates are fixed by the Governor in Council.

I was suggesting to the minister that if a man leased a wharf he might be permitted to make his own

schedule, subject t-o the control of the Railway Commission.
The rates would be fixed by the order in council.

We have lost two hours over a Bill which might have been put through in half an hour if proper preparation had been made. The minister tells us that this is an experiment. We do not want experiments. This matter had not come under public attention, but now that it has come before the House a certain amount of attention has been drawn to it. Bills have often been introduced in this House and allowed to stand over for a year. If that were done in the present case, no harm would result and good would be done. I can well understand that the minister wants to get the power he is asking for. But first let him get control of all the wharfs. Between now and next session let him take an inventory and let his officers report as to every wharf. Then next session let him bring down to parliament the information that parliament has a right to have, that members may know what they are doing. Then let the minister bring down, not a statute such as this, which is virtually a direction to the government to do whatever they like in the matter, but a statute which embodies the main conditions under which these wharfs should be dealt with. As to the lease, let us have not a mere promise, vague and unwritten, but the necessary conditions of the lease, so tliat in this statute, as in other statutes, the terms upon which this public property is to be handed over should be known and understood. Among other things, that the rights of the public may be safeguarded let it be provided that after the wharf is under the control of any lessee all persons should have the right to use it upon reasonable specified terms. With this before us we can put through a statute in half an hour, and do it intelligently, and do it in a way to respond to the duties we owe to our people. As it is now, we cannot do that. I ask the minister to let this stand over until next session. None of these wharfs will run away-of course, some of them may be swept away-in the meantime-
Business will not stand still. If the minister is seized of the situation, he can bring down amendments to the Bill this session.
After the discussion I can realize what my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) is asking.
I do not agree with the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. J. A. Currie). I think that hasty legislation is worse than no legislation. The law now on the statute-book has been there un-
changed for twenty-five years, as I understand it. No great harm will be done by waiting another year. The minister, if necessary, can make temporary arrangements with parties in the meantime.
I have no power.

Ministers often do things they have no power to do. It can be done all right. I appeal to the minister, in the interests of the public to let the matter stand. It will go to the public, and their attention will be attracted to it. Next session we can have before us a great deal of information which we have not now. I venture the opinion that very few members have any instructions from their constituents in regard to the matter. The public generally do not know there is such a Bill before the House. But, with the information that we ought to have, next session we can put through a good Bill and do it quickly.
Progress reported.

House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to authorize the Governor in Council to enter into a contract or cc ntracts for a term not exceeding ten years with any individual or company, for the performance of a steamship service between a port or ports in Canada and a French port ci ports, on such terms and conditions as the Governor in Council deems expedient, and to grant therefor a subsidy not exceeding two hundred thousand dollars a year, based upon a minimum service of fifteen round voyages a year, and a subsidy therefor not exceeding one hundred thousand dollars, and so in﻿4437

proportion for a more frequent service.-Mr. Erodeur.
Would the minister explain how these two sums work out ? There is first a subsidy of $200,000 a year, based, as I understand it upon fifteen round voyages.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. P. BRODEUR (Minister of Marine and Fisheries).
speechtext: If my hon friend (Mr. Lennox) will permit me, I will explain it. Last year we passed legislation of the same character as this; but this year, instead of taking power to make only one contract, we take power to make one or several contracts. Last year legislation was passed for the purpose of enabling the Governor in Council to pay a subsidy to the Allen Line, which is doing the service between France and Canada, and it was contended that the fact that we had made a contract for only one year precluded the government from making another contract. We did not intend to make a contract for a long period, in view of the fact that we did not know whether the French parliament would ratify the treaty. But now that the treaty has been passed by the Senate, who were formerly objecting to it, we expect it will come into force very soon. We therefore take power this year, not only to make a contract for the present year, but to make a contract for a period not exceeding ten years. Then, whereas we provided by statute last year a sum of $5,555 for each trip, this year we propose to improve the service, and for that purpose to give a mimimum sum of $6,666.66 per trip. Those are the two changes made; first, we take power to renew the contract at discretion, instead of being obliged to come to parliament next year for new; authority; and in the second place, instead of giving $5,500 a year, we propose to give $6,600.
On that basis, for 15 trips, it will be in all $200,000?
Yes.

I do not notice anything about the size of the boats, or their capacity, or the tonnage. Should there not be provision that the boats shall be of a certain tonnage, and some guarantee of the quality of the service?
The conditions my hon. friend mentions have never been heretofore put in the Bill. It is provided however, that instead of having a 10 knot service as at present, we will have a 12 knot service.	.
You think it is unnecessary to specify any minimum of tonnage for the boats?

That is provided for in (the contract. The hon. gentleman will
find the conditions of the contract in the report of the Trade and Commerce Department.

I presume the purpose is to promote trade between France and Canada as a consequence of the present French treaty. Could the minister tell us if France is giving a like amount, or what amount is she giving on her part to promote commerce between the two countries.

The French government proceeds in a different manner from ours, it encourages shipping from its ports by the payment of a certain sum of money to vessels plying to other ports. In Canada we subsidize a mail service between different countries and our own, but in France they subsidize the boats themselves. I am told, however, but not officially, that perhaps the French government will put on a line of their own between Canada and France.

I assume the object of this subsidy is to promote trade between France and Canada. We wish to find better markets in other countries for the products of the Canadian farms and industries. I notice that the difference between our exports to France and our imports from France last year is very great. If we are going to derive no greater trade advantage than we have done in the past, it seems to me that we are paying a very large sum of money for something that is not of great value. I notice, in the answer made by the Minister of Customs to a question of the hon. member for North Toronto, that for the year ending 31st March, 1908, our imports from France totalled $10,251,717, while our exports amounted to only $1,806,732. Now, it doesjseem to me that we are simply providing a means of furnishing a market in Canada for the people of France, instead of doing what I think we ought to do, trying to find a market in France for the products of Canada. If there is to be no great advantage by reason of the French treaty-and I must confess that I have very little faith that we aTe going to derive any material advantage, even if we get the minimum tariff of France-if we are not going to change the relative difference between imports and exports very much, Canada is certainly paying a very high price for the privilege of trading with France. We are practically paying $200,000 a year to enable France to come into our markets to the extent of $10,251,717, while all the advantage we get in return is that we are able to send to France $1,806,732. I think the aim of the government should be to find new markets for Canada, instead of continuing the policy of finding new markets in Canada for every other country in the world. I think thi

government has absolutely failed in carrying out the promises that were made to us many years ago, that they were going to find new markets for Canada. We have heard a great deal about the sixty million market in the United States, but practically the promise made in that respect has never materialized. We heard a good deal about the Japanese treaty; I am not aware that we have secured, for the products of the soil at any rate, any advantage from that treaty, although we have given to Japan very material advantages in our markets. The same in regard to the French treaty. Whilst we permit the people of France to trade with us on certain terms under this French treaty, we extend the same terms to some twelve or thirteen other countries from which we receive no concessions. We should think seriously before we throw away $200,000 a year for such a very small advantage to Canada. I think we are paying very dear for the privilege of trading with the French republic. Surely the government must have some assurance that our market in France is going to be very materially increased before they would feel warranted in asking parliament to pay out $200,000 a year for such a trifling advantage. I have not looked at the schedules of the French treaty during the past year, but my recollection is that there is very little in those schedules that will inure to the benefit of Canada or enable us to get into their markets on favourable terms. Their tariff is so high that I do not think we would be able to get over it, and I certainly hesitate to support a resolution to give away $200,000 a year largely for the purpose of finding a market for French products in Canada. It is easy to throw open our doors and ask people to come and trade with us, but surely the policy of the government should be rather to find markets for Canadian products than to open the Canadian market to the goods of every other country. We have a British preference now which provides a market in Canada for the products of Great Britain and nothing was ever done by the government to assist us in getting a better entry into the British market. The Minister of Agriculture even failed to secure the removal of the embargo on cattle, which would have been a tremendous boon to the people of Canada. I doubt if the minister will be able to do anything along that line owing to the stand he and other members of the government, especially the Prime Minister, have taken, in educating the people of Great Britain to believe that we do not want anything in return for the preference.
It looks to me almost as if we were making a free gift to France. Are we to pay $200,000 a year to enable us to give them that gift absolutely free? Not only are we going to open our doors to them and furnish a market for their products, but we are Mr. HENDERSON.
practically going to pay the transportation charges on their products into our country. What material advantage is that to the people of Canada? Even suppose we do get wine a few cents a gallon cheaper, we have the grapes in this country and we could manufacture the light wines in sufficient quantities for our own use. There may be a few items like silk which are put down at a low rate of duty, so that we could get them more cheaply. But silks are not very expensive in Canada and the people of Canada could afford to buy them on the ordinary terms. I do not think it would pay us to give a bounty of $200,000 a year in order to get silk and wines and a few other articles cheaper from France than we have been getting them. I cannot see. my way to support this resolution. I think we are paying too much for the whistle, and I hope the minister will have some explanation to give to us which will show that there will be an advantage to Canada commensurate with the large amount of money we are paying. In ten years this subsidy would amount to $2,000,000, a very considerable sum. We talk about millions now as though they did not amount to anything, but we have to provide a great many millions in order to carry on our government and we must be careful of our millions because when they are multiplied by tens they become a serious charge. I hope the minister, before pressing this resolution, will be able to show us that we are going to get something in return for the large amount we are called upon to pay out.

If the government did not think that this resolution would improve the commercial relations between Canada and France, we would certainly not have introduced it. This is not a new policy, it has been in existence for many years. The first legislation subsidizing a line of steamships between Canada and France was passed in 1884. The Act of that year provided for a weekly service between Canada and Great Britain, calling at a French port, and offered a subsidy of $500,-
000.	In 1894 another statute was passed increasing that subsidy to $750,000. In 1896 provision was made for a weekly service with a subsidy of $750,000 and a section was added providing for a five-years' contract, and a fortnightlv service between Canada, France and Belgium at a yearly subsidy of $50,000. This was increased to $100,000 in 1901. Nothing was done even under this offer of $100,000 until a few years after this subsidy had been on the statute book. At last the Allan line agreed to undertake that service and for some years past they have been performing it.
They were doing it previously for $100,000 a year.

Yes, but they were giving only a tri-weekly service with slow

boats, and the proposal now is, to increase the payment for each trip from $5,500 to $6,600.
Is the French government aiding in this subsidy ?

The policy of the French government is to subsidize the construction of the steamers, but they have no subsidy similar to that which we pay in Canada. Some years ago there was informal negotiation with a view of the French government contributing to this subsidy but the question came up as to under what lias the ships should sail and it was found impossible to reach an agreement. My hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) has spoken of the trade between Canada and France, and I might point out that the treaty of 1893 included but a very few articles which were subject to the French minimum tariff.
What ports will be served by this line ?
Quebec and Montreal in summer, and St. John in winter.
What ports on the other side ?

Havre. UndeT the treaty of 1897 with France, a very long list of Canadian goods will be allowed into France under the minimum tariff, and in return we have given to some 80 articles of French production the benefit of the intermediate tariff. My hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) is not sure that we will derive any benefit from the French treaty but I hold a contrary opinion. In view of the fact that before the treaty of 1907 Canadian goods generally had to pay the very high maximum tariff and came into competition with goods from countries contiguous to France which paid only the minimum tariff, it was impossible for us to do any extensive trade with France. It is natural to expect, now that Canadian goods have the benefit of the minimum tariff, that there will be a laTge development of Canadian trade with France. Indeed, since the establishment of this steamship line, and notwithstanding all the difficulties that had to be encountered in the past, we have increased our trade to some extent. There are many commodities which we might export to France with profit. There are some other articles of fish that we could export to France. Now we are having the benefit of the minimum tariff on our fish we may also expect to sell more of that product in France.
How much lower is the rate on lobsters than was the rate under the tariff of 1893?
It is the same.
Well then we do not expect to get any advantage.

No, but I was telling my hon. friend that under the treaty of 1893 we have been exporting lobsters there and we may expect, when we are enjoying the minimum tariff, not only on that article but also on 150 other articles, that the development of trade which has taken place in regard to that specific article will also occur with respect to the other articles which are mentioned in the treaty.
Could the minister tell us the value of the lobsters shipped to France ?
$500,000 or $600,000 worth, if not more.
Over $600,000 worth.
I think perhaps it is over $600,000 worth.
Then that would be about one-third of the whole shipment to France.

Precisely, but my hon. friend has not caught the argument that I am trying to make. I say that we have been able, due to the fact that we have a minimum tariff on this article, to develop a large trade with France. Now, _we have the minimum tariff not only on this article but on 150 other articles which we are producing in this country. Take, for instance, cheese, butter and other products of the farm.
What is the tariff on cheese and butter ?

On cheese, 25 francs maximum and 12 and 15 francs minimum. The tariff on butter is 20 francs minimum and 30 francs maximum. It was absolutely impossible for us to compete with regard to butter or cheese with Denmark which is enjoying the benefit of the minimum tariff.

I would like the minister to state whether the government have made any calculation as to the quantity of farm products that we may expect in the coming years to export from Canada to France under the new treaty?

I do not know whether any calculations have been made by the Department of Finance or not. I have not got them under my hand, but I may mention a case which was brought to my notice when I was in France two years ago in connection with this treaty showing the great advantage it would be to us to enjoy the benefit of the minimum tariff. It has reference to the export of hams. I got this information from a gentleman _ who had been importing from Canada to France. He told me that at one time he was doing a very fine business with France because there was only one duty. Ham was not enjoying any minimum tariff so that

we were in the same position as competing European countries which are neighbours of France. He told me that in 1903, I think, they changed their tariff in France and put on hams a maximum and minimum tariff. The result was that the countries which had treaties with France, like Austria, Russia, Germany, Switzerland, Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Spain and Italy, could export their ham at the minimum rate while we had to pay the maximum rate. This business was lost to the Canadians and this firm which had established a very fine business between France and Canada was obliged to cease business in that line. What is the situation under the new treaty? Under the new treaty we enjoy the benefit of the minimum tariff so that we will be in the same position in France as that occupied by our European competitors. We expect to develop a business which has been absolutely killed by the absence of a treaty.

Perhaps my hon. friend could get these statistics, if they are made up in the Finance Department or in the Trade and Commerce Department, end give them when the Bill is under discussion and let us pass the resolution and have the Bill introduced before six o'clock.
I will inquire in the Department of Trade and Commerce whether they have these figures.

When the treaty was passed the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) (promised to make an effort to prevent the importation of absinthe. I would like to know if any progress has been made along that line or if there is any hope of that change being made. I noticed a short time ago that Germany had taken steps to prohibit the importation of absinthe into their country. Also with regard to the importation of wines, there is great danger that we may ruin our own wine business because we can raise all the grapes we require. It would be important to know whether steps have been taken in these directions.

We probably will have to introduce this session some legislation with regard to the approval of the change which has been made in the treaty and I will draw the attention of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance to the question which has been put by my hon. friend from Dufferin.
I hope the minister will do so in very strong terms for I do think the danger from the introduction of absinthe is greater than any advantage which we receive from this Bill.

Is it contemplated to have any control over the freight rates in connection with these boats?
Mr. BROrEUR.

There has been an undertaking by the company and it was stipulated in the contract which was passed last year that the rates between Havre and Canada shall be the same as those between Havre and New York.

Before this resolution passes, I think this would be an opportune time to bring to the notice of the hon. minister and the government the great necessity which exists for a port of call in Nova Scotia for those lines in the summer time. Take this proposed line of steamers which ply between Montreal and Quebec and some port in France, we are told by the hon. minister that fish, particularly lobsters, is one of our largest exports to France. It would therefore be a great boon to Cape Breton and the coast of Nova Scotia if we had a port somewhere in the Province to which these steamers would call and on which we could ship our fish and other exports to France, where there' is an excellent market for them. These steamers will pass by our doors practically within a few miles, and it will be too bad if provision be not made for them to call at North Sydney. At that port there is considerable French trade. It is the headquarters of the French trawlers, a trade which has only been developed the last few years. These steamers also take a large quantity of coal, and it would be much cheaper for them to purchase it at North Sydney rather than at Montreal or Quebec. If they were to call at North Sydney, they would there get their bunker much more expeditiously and cheaply, which would be an inducement to them to call there. What I have said regarding this new line between Canada and France also applies to the steamers plying between Canada and Mexico. In the maritime provinces, we have no chance of communicating with those lines unless they call somewhere on the coast of Nova Scotia, and North Sydney is 'the nearest point and not at all out of their way. The English mail has been landed there, and if that does not put the mail steamers much out of their course, the delay would be still less of a disadvantage in the case of freight boats. Besides North Sydney being the terminus of the Intercolonial Railway, it u'ould become the point of shipping for the whole province of Nova Scotia and the provinces of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island during the summer thus giving to those provinces the advantage of the French market. In winter of course the steamers will go to St. John, but in the summer we have no better means of accommodating them than by their calling at North Sydney, which would give us the advantage of shipping to the French and the Mexican markets, and give them the advantage of cheaper coal. I do not

think I would be justified in allowing this opportunity to pass without bringing this matter to the notice of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
