Bill (No. 110) respecting agricultural fertilizers.-Mr. Templeman. Read the second time and House went into committee there-cn.
On section 1,

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The present law respecting agricultural fertilizers, which has been on the statute-book, I believe, for twenty years, has been found inoperative and ineffective to secure the object for which it was passed, that is, to^protect the purchasers of agricultural fertilizers. It is proposed to repeal the existing Act absolutely, replacing it by the Bill now before the House. The present law requires the manufacturers to submit their fertilizers to the Department of Inland Revenue for analysis. The Department of Inland Revenue publishes in bulletins the results of these analyses. These bulletins are supposed to inform the farmers or purchasers of the quality of the fertilizers. The manufacturers are required by the law to send in their samples for analysis in the month of January. As a matter of fact the samples this year did not arrive in the department very'much before February or March and before the issue of the bulletin in April this year the farmers had already purchased all they required for the year and the work ot the department was useless.
Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Because the analysis was made too late.
The Act provides that they shall.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: But they don't do it; and even if it comes in in the month of January, the bulletin could not be got out in time to place the evidence before the purchasers and enable them to judge from the analyses the value of the fertilizers they are purchasing. At all events, it has been found after years of experience that the issuance of these bulletins, with the analyses of the department, has not accomplished the object for which they were issued, that is, to inform the farmers of the character of the fertilizers placed on the market. The new Act is a radical change. We do not propose to analyse for the manufacturers. The law as it exists has been altogether in the interest of the manufacturer rather than of the purchaser. The department has been analysing these samples all these years for $3, whereas it costs the department $7 to make an analysis of a fertilizer.
What was this chapter of the old Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I think it is 132. We propose under the Act now before the House to require the manufacturers to register their brand with the department, they will receive a number, and they will sell their brand of fertilizer under a distinctive number. That is necessary

from the fact that many of the fertilizers now on the market have names very similar, so that in the event of prosecutions for failing to live up to the guarantee they are supposed to give of the merit of their fertilizers, it is hard to distinguish what particular fertilizer was bought, because there are so many of practically the same name. It is proposed that every manufacturer should receive a registered number under which he will sell his fertilizer, the trade mark and the name of the brand. We propose that he shall himself place on the label or tag of the fertilizer a guaranteed analysis of the component parts of the article; that is, the manufacturer shall put on the parcel, bag or box, as it may be, a guaranteed analysis of the fertilizer. That is the main principle of the Bill. Then when it is on the market we can collect samples, and by analysis ascertain whether the manufacturer is living up to his guaranteed analysis as published by himself.
Did the minister say that the manufacturers' goods were only analysed once a year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: No, I did not say that. Under the proposed Bill the manufacturer will place upon the bag, or box, or tin can of the fertilizer he is selling, a label with the name of the brand, the registration number, the name and address of the manufacturer, and an analysis as guaranteed by him, which analysis will show the percentages. A guaranteed analysis means the valuation of a fertilizer in terms of its contents of phosphoric acid, nitrogen and potash. They would place that on the label, and they must live up to that guaranteed analysis. All the fertilizers they place on the market must be of the value which they guarantee. Samples will be collected from the dealers from time to time, and will be analysed, and we will thereby ascertain whether the manufacturer is living up to his guaranteed analysis as published.

I understood the minister to say that under the old Act the manufacturers have their goods analysed only once a year; will the minister tell us how often their goods are likely to be examined under the new Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
In the first place, the manufacturer must publish with his goods the analysis thereof, so that every purchaser can read it. The department will then from time to time procure samples of the fertilizers on the market and analyse them, and ascertain if the manufacturer is living up to his guaranteed analysis. A farmer purchasing any particular fertilizer may, under the Act, procure an analysis of a sample of the fertilizer; therefore any Mr. TEMPLEMAN.
particular brand of fertilizer may be analysed as often as samples are sent in to the department.
Then you will publish in a bulletin the results of analyses of the different samples you have gathered?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes.
Will any farmer have a right to send down samples to be examined without charge?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Not without charge. The charge in the Bill is $5.
Couldn't that charge be much cut down?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The actual cost to the department of analysing a sample of fertilizer is $7. It is a difficult analysis to make. Section 10, providing for the fee, reads thus:
Any purchaser of a registered fertilizer may obtain from the minister an analysis of the fertilizer as delivered to him, by making application for such analysis accompanied by a sample of the fertilizer of at least one pound weight and taken in accordance with the directions given in schedule B to this Act, and on payment of a fee of $5.
The House will readily understand that if there was no fee or only a very small fee imposed, the department would- be flooded with requests for analyses. The inspectors will send in the samples and the results of the analysis will be published in a bulletin. It will then be known whether the manufacturer is living up to his guarantee, and if he is not there is a penalty provided.
If a farmer sends in a sample and the analysis does not agree with the statement published by the manufacturer, who will prosecute?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Under section 12 it it is the duty of our own officers to collect samples and if the analysis proves that the fertilizer is not up to standard we prosecute. Although this Act does not provide for prosecutions when a sample is sent in by a farmer or any person other than an officer of the department, I would be of opinion myself that in the event of a sample being found deficient it would be the duty of the department to prosecute.
Would it not be well to have that provision included in the Bill?
What officers will be appointed under this Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The inspectors under this Act will be the same as the inspectors under the Adulteration of Food Act. It is not the intention of this Act to appoint any new or special officers.
If a farmer wanted to send in a sample, his most convenient way would be to hand the five dollar fee and his sample to an inspector.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The most convenient way would be to get the inspector of food to take the sample.

I would assume from the statement of the minister that if a farmer were suspicious that a manufacturer was selling a fertilizer which was not up to the government standard, all he need do is to write to the inspector and the inspector would take samples.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: There is no standard fixed by the government. The standard is fixed by the manufacturer, who places that standard on a printed label on the package guaranteeing his own product as being equal to that standard. He must live up to that, so that the purchaser knows what he is buying.
What was the original charge for analysis?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Three dollars.

It seems to me that the manufacturer who is putting immense quantities of fertilizers on the market, should at least be compelled to pay the full fee when samples are analysed in the public interest. The weak spot in the Inspection of Food Act is that the fines imposed are not heavy enough, and I believe that will be found to be the weak spot in this Act. Fraudulent manufacturers should be fined sufficient to pay for the operation of all the machinery for carrying out the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The Bill proposes to protect farmers without any cost to them whatever. The manufacturer pays $2 for registration and an annual license fee of $5 for selling, and as we do not analyse for the manufacturer under this Bill we do not charge; he has got to do the analysing himself.

Suppose he puts a sample on the market that is not up to the standard, what protection is there for the farmer? The farmer who buys a small quantity is not going to pay $5 and send the sample down to Ottawa to be analysed.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: It is the duty of the department to collect samples of every fertilizer on the market and to analyse the same to know whether the manufacturer is living up to his own guaranteed analysis. We do not debar persons from collecting samples.and sending them in, but in that case we propose a fee of $5.
It would shut them off.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
It would deter many, but if a farmer or other person buys a large quantity of fertilizer and has reason to
think that it' is not up to the standard, a fee of $5 is not prohibitive.
Would it not be fairer if, in case a farmer sends in a sample and it it is proven that it is not up to the guarantee, the manufacturer and not the farmer should pay the fee?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: In the case of a prosecution of a manufacturer by an officer of the department, or by a private individual, as the result of an analysis made by the department, there is a penalty of $50 provided under clause 15.
But it would be fairer that the farmer should not be called upon to pay the fee if the article is not up to the standard.

It might be. I da not think that, under this Bill, there will be many prosecutions by private individu als. Nor do I think there will be many analyses made at the request of individuals. There are only two or three hundred fertilizers all told on the market. It would not be difficult for the department to analyse one or two samples of each kind every year and publish the result.
How will the work of the inspection be carried on?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Under the Adulteration of Food Act there are fifteen or sixteen inspectors. As I said a moment ago, that word ' inspector ' is a misnomer. These men are officers of the department with other duties to perform. When instructed they purchase samples of food and divide each sample into two, sending one part to Ottawa and leaving the other with the vendor. The vendor knows that the sample is to be analysed, and if it is not up to the requirements he is liable to be prosecuted. One inspector or purchaser of samples of fertilizers could in one week collect samples of all the fertilizers sold in Ontario.
The danger is that manufacturers may be sending out to retail dealers all over the province stuff that is not up to the standard, but the inspector inspects that which he finds in the factory

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: If the manufacturer sends out fertilizer not up to the standard, he is liable to punishment.
The minister will see that there is a clause applying to fertilizers made to order and not intended for sale.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Of course.

The only person this law can get after is the manufacturer. And it is provided that the sample must be taken 'in the presence of the manufacturer

or his agent.' Why not make the vendor responsible, as well as the manufacturer ? If you do that, the vendor will see to it that he is getting the right article in the first place. As the hon. member for Dufferin (Mr. Barr) suggests, suppose there is dishonesty or collusion between the manufacturer and the retailer there is nothing to prevent the manufacturer making an arrangement under which he could give out a fraudulent fertilizer. After the fertilizer has left the manufacturer's hands and gone into that of the dealer, there is no machinery in the Act to provide for the prosecution of either the manufacturer or the dealer.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Every fertilizer is sold under a registered number, and that carries back to the manufacturer, who is the party who ought to be prosecuted. My hon. friend spoke of making the vendor liable. Under the Adulteration of Foods Act, one of the difficulties is that the innocent dealer is held liable for the adulteration of the manufacturer in many cases. I appeal to the House that the guilty party is the manufacturer rather than the innocent seller ?
But how do you catch him? Suppose he is an American manufacturer ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Under section 4, every foreign manufacturer has to appoint a resident agent in Canada who, for all the purposes of this law, is regarded as a manufacturer.

But the minister will notice that the sample must be taken 'in the presence of the manufacturer or his agent.' How can a farmer go into the factory and take a sample of the fertilizer in the presence of the manufacturer or his agent? If you were to say that the registration number is prima facie evidence that the article was made by me manufacturer represented by that number, and if the vendor proved that he purchased it from the manufacturer, he should be free, you could follow it up on that line. But you bar out everything of this kind by providing that the samples must be taken in the presence of the manufacturer or his agent.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I have here an amendment which I shall propose that samples must be taken ' in the presence of the vendor or his agent.1

Suppose the manufacturer in Toronto turns out these goods, sells them to a wholesale dealer in Winnipeg, who sells them to a retailer in Calgary, through whom they finally find their way into the hands of a farmer in that section of the country- In case of a violation of this law in the case of those goods, where would the trial take place? If the manufacturer is to be prosecuted, do you propose to go Mr. J. A. CURRIE.
out to the place where the purchaser lives to collect your evidence? I am afraid there will be a great deal of difficulty in enforcing this law.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Because the prosecution in that case should be of the manufacturer.
At Toronto?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: At Toronto, and the material evidence is found in the city of Ottawa by the analyst who makes the analysis and proves that it is not up to the standard. The inspector who makes the purchase would be a material witness in a case of that kind. This Bill throws the onus on the manufacturer to live up to his guaranteed analysis.

How would you get your evidence to substantiate the fact that the farmer purchased the identical goods and that he sent the identical goods down to your department for analysis? You would have to bring the retailer, the wholesaler and the farmer down to enable you to produce your evidence.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Not at all.
Mr, LENNOX. What section is it that throws the liability on the manufacturer?
Section 15.
I do not read it in that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Every person who sells or offers or exposes for sale-
That certainly includes the manufacturer.

That is not what the minister said I understood him correctly. I would not take that to mean what the minister said a moment ago. I do not know what the minister's aim is. I understood the minister to say that the object of this Bill was to throw the liability upon the manufacturer. Section 15 provides that:
Every person who sells or offers or exposes fcr sale-
That is not limited to the manufacturer, or the first purchaser or the second purchaser or any intermediate purchaser. It applies to every purchaser who happens to sell this article, from the manufacturer down to the last retail dealer. Would not that be the case? Is that what the minister intends?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes, the intention is to make the manufacturer liable if his guaranteed analysis as printed on the label is not lived up to.
That is quite true. I understand that part of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Every sample of fertilizer as sold under a number, it is regis-

tered, the manufacturer's name is on it, his guaranteed analysis is on the label and if it does not comply with the guaranteed analysis he may be prosecuted under section 15. If it is not clear that section 15 refers to the manufacturer, then we will make it so because that is the intention.

While I think it is quite clear that it does include the manufacturer, I think it is also quite clear that it includes everybody else who sells the fertilizer. If the minister does not intend to include any one but the manufacturer I think an amendment would be necessary. It certainly does include the manufacturer but it includes a great many others as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I do not know that we should confine it absolutely to the manufacturer. It may be that after it leaves the manufacturer and passes through two or three hands some person may manipulate the goods.

Do you not think that a heavier penalty should be inflicted upon the manufacturer for selling, because he knows what he puts into it, than upon some innocent purchaser who bought it on the strength of the tag attached to it and who believed it to contain the full percentage.
Mr, TEMPLEMAN. I want to move an amendment to paragraph (d) of section 2, being the definition of the word ' agent.' 1 am afraid that the definition as printed is too general. I propose to substitute the following.
Agent means any person whose name has teen filed with the department as provided by section 4 of this Act.
An agent under this Act means the representative of a foreign manufacturer and not a retail merchant who may be selling fertilizers.
Why do you say ' foreign ' manufacturer?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: He must have an agent in Canada to represent him.
Yes, but there are a lot of fertilizers being manufactured in Canada. For instance, there is the production of phosphate and almost every slaughter house is manufacturing fertilizers.

In case a farmer, or any one purchasing a fertilizer, has good reason to believe that the article he has purchased from the manufacturer is not up to the standard as designated by the tag, if he notifies the inspector, giving his reasons, would it not be the duty of the inspector to come and take samples?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Unquestionably, and if any farmer has reason to think that any fertilizer is not up to the analysis he can notify the inspector or, better still, notify
the department in Ottawa which would instruct the inspector to secure samples of that particular fertilizer. It is important that the inspector, or whoever purchases, must do it in such a way that he can give evidence in court that the specimen he bought was a specimen of the particular fertilizer and the specimen that he sent to Ottawa to be analysed and then our analyst proves in court that it is not up to the standard.
If the sample were taken under such circumstances by the inspector would you still charge the farmer $5 for analysis?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: No. The $5 fee imposed by this Act is more to guard against the department being flooded with requests for analyses that are really unnecessary than anything else. We will analyse all the samples that are necessary if no person sends them in, but still we want to leave it open to any person to send in a sample if he wishes. The department has been flooded with requests for work of this kind. We do a great deal of analytical work in the laboratory and it is necessary to put a check upon it in some way. It is not necessary in this Act that we should make a free analysis of all the fertilizers.

A farmer has to pay $5 for an analysis, but what is going to arouse his attention to the fact that a certain fertilizer is not up to standard? How is he to determine whether there is anything wrong with it or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: He ought to have some reason for sending in a sample to be analysed. What is going to arouse his attention, I do not know, unless he has used it for several years with poor results.
There will be no use then in throwing away $5 to have it analysed. He would simply not buy any more of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The Act supposes that every fertilizer put on the market must be analysed by the department and the result printed in a bulletin, and the farmer will know from this analysis, whether the particular fertilizer he has bought is up to the standard or not.

When a man buys a box or sack of a certain fertilizer, it is impossible for him to tell whether it is up to the standard or not, and I fail to see how he is to get the information which will enable him to do so.

TAYLOR I think the present Bill better than the old one, because the manufacturer under the old one, could send a sample to the department and have it analysed and a bulletin issued showing that it was manufactured up to such a brand.

Then he might manufacture an adulterated article and put it on the market. Of course, he can do that now but is liable to be caught, because the department will be likely to analyse it.
Would not the sample to be analysed be similar to the samples of the jellies and jams?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: It will be sampled the same way.

The department is collecting these every day, and I do not think there will be any difficulty in that respect. Would it be possible to raise the standard of fertilizers that are manufactured and make them come up to a standard fixed by the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: We do not attempt to fix any standard. The manufacturer himself fixes the standard by printed analysis. I am also advised it would be very difficult to fix a standard for any particular fertilizer. There would have to be scores of standards according to the different characters of the different soils. A certain soil might require a fertilizer containing more nitrogen or more phosphoric acid and so on. We require that the manufacturer shall state distinctly what constituents are in his fertilizer and he must live up to that standard, and the purchaser judges whether the paiticular number is the quality he wants. The standard is created by the manufacturer and all we do is to compel him to live up to his own standard.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The discussion is too general. The Bill should be taken clause by clause. Section 2 is now under consideration, and there is an amendment moved to subsection (d) providing that the words ' not a manufacturer who sells or offers for sale any fertilizer ' be struck out, and in its stead the following inserted:
Agent means any person whose name has been filed with the minister as provided by section 4 of the Act.
Should we not define the word ' vendor '?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I do not think the word ' vendor ' need be defined at all. The word ' agent ' refers solely to a person appointed by a foreign manufacturer to represent him in Canada.
In the Bill as printed the word ' agentJ meant vendor. Is that intended?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: No.
Then, under schedule B, there will be no method by which we can attack the seller.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
We are going to change schedule B.
Section 2 as amended, agreed to.

On section 3,
Fertilizers shall be considered as distinct brands, when differing either in guaranteed compositions, trade mark, name or in any other characteristic method of marking.

We have been discussing whether a certain standard could not be devised. I think it would not be wise to have a standard set because any manufacturer can describe the standard on the back of the package, and according to the quality the price will be fixed. I would be perfectly satisfied with that.
On section 4,-Name of Foreign Manufacturer's Agent or Representative in Canada to be filed with the minister.
What is to prevent the manufacturer from putting up a man of straw as his agent?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: It is hardly probable that a large manufacturer would put up a man of straw as his agent, considering that he has to register every year and get his license to sell. He might do it once, but he could not do it a second time, because he could not get his license to sell in Canada again.
In some subsequent part of the Bill is there provision for prosecuting the agent instead of the foreign manufacturer?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The object of section 4 is to require the foreign manufacturer to name an agent in Canada who registers and who can be proceeded against, I assume, as the representative of the foreign manufacturers.

I would not like to 'assume ' about it, but I would like to know from the minister if there is provision ia the law for reaching the agent. I have not paid very close attention to the measure, but I have not seen any provision under which we can reach the agent in that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I inferred that the agent of the foreign manufacturer could be proceeded against. If it should appear, when we have gone through the Bill that that is not the case, we can make an amendment. The object of having an agent appointed is to have the representative of the manufacturer where he can be reached.

I do not wish to embarrass the minister, but he will understand that we cannot leave a matter of this kind to mere probability. I do not know of anything in'the Bill to enable us to deal with the agent. Section 15 provides that the person who offers or exposes for sale may be prosecuted. Unless under that clause, I do not see any way in which we

can deal with the agent. Will that cover it?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I think so. Under section 2, ' guaranteed analysis ' means the valuation of a fertilizer by a manufacturer or agent in terms of its content of phosphoric acid, nitrogen and potash. It seems to me that the agent would be liable to prosecution as the representative of the foreign manufacturer who gave this 'guaranteed analysis/ However, that is a legal point on which I would not care to be too positive. We can make the point clearer if necessary.

We all know that frauds are being perpetrated on the farmers right along in these fertilizers, and that is the reason why this Bill is before us. Suppose that a bunch of these fraudulent dealers in fertilizers in the United States get together and call themselves the Diamond Fertilizing Company. They send a sample of their brand to Canada, and it is analysed by the department and proved of high value. A man from Buffalo or from Chicago, perhaps unknown to fame, is appointed to act as agent, and establishes himself in an office that is not too conspicuous. With the certificate of analysis given by the department, the representatives of this brand go all over the country and sell large quantities, because they have a certificate, and because they are underselling the dealers here. All the material sold comes into Canada within a week. After ten days or two weeks an analysis is incidentally made with a sample taken by the inspector. But by this time the machinery of the department is put in motion, the * agent ' is out of the country and all the small storekeepers and dealers are left loaded up with worthless fertilizers. Then, the same gang get together again to put out, let us say the ' lightning ' brand, and puts it through the same process. These methods have been carried on in other lines of business, and even manufacturers have been swindled in this way. This is done, for instance, with a brand of steel. This material is sold all over the country, perhaps at fifty cents a pound, and when the man gets his five or ten or twenty pounds, he finds that it is not better than wrought iron. But what I would suggest is that any foreign company appointing an agent in this country should be called upon to deposit with the Inland Revenue Department at least $500 as a guarantee of good faith, so that if they turn out to be a fraud you will have something.

I should think the common law would cover that. In any case, a manufacturer would hardly appoint an agent for the purpose of defrauding decent people. Certainly such a thing is unknown in my experience in business.

The hon. member (Mr. Beattie) knows very well that fully 50 per cent of the goods sold in the United States by manufacturers, so-called, are not manufactured by these people. The goods of Smith, Jones & Robinson, ' manufacturers,' may be all made in the same place.
That is a different thing. But the manufacturer who sends out a brand of goods expects to continue in the business and he would not spoil his reputation for the sake of selling a few hundred dozen.

This Bill is designed to prevent a specific kind of fraud, fraud that has been committed on the farmers so often and so widely that the government deems it necessary to pass special legislation on the subject. As to nine-tenths of these brands of fertilizers, there is not even an office at the headquarters of the so-called factory.

But it would ruin the manufacturer's business to send out an inferior article. If I were a manufacturer I certainly would not send out a spurious article if I intended to remain in business.
Mr, SAMUEL SHARPE. I think the difficulty could be met if the minister would adopt the suggestion of my hon. friend from North Simcoe, and make the agent subject to all the pains and penalties of a defaulting foreign manufacturer. If the agent is subject to these liabilities, he will stand between the manufacturer and the public, he is a guarantee and protection to the public.
Another thing the minister might do is not to license or appoint an agent unless he is a responsible man.

Here is where I see a difficulty. An agent sells goods in wholesale lots to a druggist, the druggist sells to a farmer, and the farmer finds that he has a lot on hand that is not up to the standard. Now how is he going to get redress? According to Schedule B, samples for analysis must be taken in the presence of the manufacturer or his agent; but the seller is not the manufacturer's agent.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
We are going to change that to vendor.
On section 6-Application for registration number.
What do you mean by 'guaranteed- analysis'?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Guaranteed analysis means the valuation of a fertilizer by the manufacturer or agent in terms of its content of phosphoric acid, nitrogen, and potash. These are the three ingredients
which I understand, compose the fertilizer. I understand these include ah the essential chemical combinations.

['As I have mentioned to the Prime Minister privately, the hour may be so far advanced that the hon. member for North Toronto would not think it desirable to bring on his motion that day. That will depend on circumstances. He is absent at present but as soon as he returns from Toronto I will ascertain from him his views and communicate with the Prime Minister.']

Your old Act provides that the samples shall contain so much ammonia, and so much phosphoric acid, and some have a combination of the two. Which one are you going to take as the standard? Because many of these fertilizers contain two ingredients in the same sample.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The manufacturer will state that on his label.
On section 7-Registration number, how affixed. Statement required.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I propose to strike out the word 'importer' so that we will deal only with the manufacturer or agent.

Again I wish to call the attention of the minister to this matter of agency. Does the minister presume to think that nobody will import a fertilizer into this country except through an agent? There is nothing to prevent me importing a fertilizer from the United States or Europe for any purpose, and selling it here, and no law will compel me to have a registered agent.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: We are passing tha* very law now.

I wish to impress upon the minister the importance of this agency. There is no use in having anybody appointed agent unless you have somebody responsible. I would suggest that when a foreign manufactured article of this description is brought into the country to be sold under guarantee, there should be a deposit made of a sum of money with the government, so that in case of default there would be something that you could lay your hand upon.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I would not care to impose conditions that would be too onerous. I think my hon. friend is too much afraid that a man of straw may be appointed an agent. I am disposed to think that any reputable manufacturer would appoint an agent of some repute, and there is little fear that the department will have to deal with that agent. We might not Tecognize him if we thought he was a man of straw. I agree that if you were to require a deposit of $500 or $100 from a manufacturer, his hona tides would be better established. But it might be that in imposing restrictions we would hamper trade when it was not necessary to do so.

I am not desirous of imposing onerous conditions. This Bill is intended to deal with reputable manufacturers, it is intended to meet a condition Mr. TEMPLEMAN.
which has existed in this country to a large extent, not only in relation to fertilizers, but to nursery stock and other matters of that kind. For instance lawn shrubs are sold all over this country as nursery stock from the Aurora Borea'is Nursery of Syracuse, or some other high sounding names. It has turned out that people nave found themselves with this stock on hand and could not get satisfaction. The minister will recognize that at there was a bona fide guarantee required the company desirous of obtaining a market here for its brand of fertilizer would willingly pay a deposit as I have suggested, whilst if it was a fraudulent concern that desired to do business, they would hesitate. When you ask a company, before they do business in this country, to appoint an agent, then you must specify that that agent must be an attorney, acting in a position of trust.
If the agent was required to be resident in Canada and acceptable to the government it -would meet the objection of my hon. friend (Mr. J. A. Currie).

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I am willing to amend it in that way.
Section 7, as amended, agreed to.
On section 4,

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I would move to add after the word ' agents ' ' acceptable to the minister and resident in Canada.'

Supposing the agent is a travelling saleman, perhaps selling drugs, who carries this as a side line, a perfectly respectable man, but not a man of financial standing, would he be considered acceptable?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: If he was a respectable man, well known in the community and vouched for, I think he would be.
But such a man might have sold $200,000 worth of fertilizer and might then leave the country. You only impose a fine and what could be done if you could not collect the fine?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Then we would lose. It is of course impossible to so regulate the sale of fertilizers or anything else that some man cannot circumvent the law.

Evidently the hon. gentleman is not a farmer or he would know that very large quantities of useless fertilizers are brought from the United States and sold to the farmers. There is great danger that an agent may be a man of straw. I am inclined to think the amendment will be an improvement, and will be some protection to the farmers against fraud of this kind. It is necessary to watch carefully the fertilizers which come from the United States.

If the hon. gentleman thinks a manufacturer is going to make an article that will only last one season, his argument is good. But if the manufacturer expects to remain in business for years to come he will not put a fraudulent article on the market. That is my experience, and I do not think the manufacturers as a rule go into business to sell an article which is a fraud on the public. I am sorry to think that we have a class of people in this country or the United States who will sell articles not up to the standard represented.

I would suggest that some such method be adopted as we adopt in British Columbia in reference to the agents of United States nursery men. In order to protect the purchaser who may not be able to get a remedy against the producer in the United States the agent has to put up a $2,000 bond, and if anything goes wrong there is a direct recourse against the agent.
In default of paying the money penalty I suppose there will be a term of imprisonment provided ? In that case the agent will see that the fine is paid and the brands kept up to grade.

If we insert the words that the agent must be acceptable to the minister it means that the minister will be responsible for the action of the agent, and if the agent is guilty of fraud the minister would have to take the responsibility.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I will take it.

Suppose I should go to the United States or to England and buy a
141j	I ; | u
brand of fertilizer from a manufacturer who has no agent in Canada, who would be responsible then? If I should prefer a certain brand of fertilizer the manufacturer of which was not represented by an agent here, I do not see why I should be prevented from buying it. Dealers do not always want to buy the same brand that everybody on the street keeps; they want if possible to sell an article that their competitors have not got.
The hon. gentleman from London (Mr. Beattie) has suggested a difficulty. Suppose a resident dealer goes to the United States and purchases goods and imports them himself, who is to be responsible?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: He cannot purchase them for sale unless there is a resident agent in Canada.
But he may become the agent as well as the importer.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
If the importer brings it into Canada he is the agent.
On section 10,
Do I understand the minister to say that the actual cost of the analysis will be $7?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: During past years it has cost $7 for each analysis of fertilizer.
I suppose you have an official in the department to do that work?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes, quite a number.
It seems a large fee.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
It is, but I am advised by the chief analyst that it costs the department more to make an analysis of fertilizers than of ordinary food stuffs.
On section 12,

I do not see that it is anybody's business to prosecute under this Act, and there does not seem to be any machinery provided for a prosecution. The report of the department, issued a couple of days ago, contains a list of a large number of samples of coffee and other articles that were found to be adulterated, but there is no machinery under the Act for punishing the people guilty of manufacturing and selling these adulterated articles. I think there should be a clause added that the inspector, if he finds the article adulterated, shall proceed against the party who is responsible under the Act. This would throw the onus on the inspector. At all events, it will then be somebody's duty to institute a prosecution.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I do not think that would be feasible. It would be the duty of the minister to prosecute, just as it is the duty of the minister now, under the

Adulteration of Foods Act, to prosecute. The knowledge of the fact that the guaranteed analysis has been violated by the manufacturer is not possessed by the inspector. The chief witness will be the chief analyst in Ottawa, who makes the analysis.
You provide that his certificate shall be taken as evidence, do you not?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes. Prosecutions, under the Adulteration of Foods Act, are by the Justice Department under instructions of the Inland Revenue Department. As a matter of fact, the number of prosecutions under that Act has not been as numerous probably as it ought to have been, for a good reason indeed. We have no food standard as yet. We have failed in some prosecutions because we had no standard. The question of fixing the standard for all food products in Canada has been engaging the attention of the department for the last year or two. It is a work of considerable magnitude to formulate a standard for all food products. At the present time the officers have the standard pretty well prepared, and we hope to put it in force by order in council under the Adulteration of Foods Act before long.

Have you got another difficulty under the Act? Formerly it was provided that you had to comply with certain provisions of the law, but as the result of an amendment made to the Inland Revenue Act some years ago I understand you could not prove your case. Therefore, prosecutions were practically dropped. This matter was brought to my attention by a prominent lawyer, and I remember discussing it in this House at some length while it was under consideration. The contention of the department was that there was nothing in it whatever, but afterwards it was franklv admitted, I think, by the minister at the head of the department, that prosecutions could not succeed because of this difficulty.	,

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: It is true that prosecutions have failed because of the fact that we have no standard. One case in particular was with respect to maple sugar or maple syrup.
I think there were more than that.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
We have had a great many analyses. We have had prosecutions, some of which succeeded and some did not. But the penalty, under the Adulteration of Foods Act, to the party adulterating, has been almost wholly from the publicity which is given to the publications of the bulletins. We are going to try to establish a standard under the Adulteration of Foods Act. We are specifying the stand-Mr. TEMPLEMAN.
ard in this Act. The standard is what the manufacturer says the article is.
You had a standard under the old Act for fertilizers. They shall not contain less than four per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: That was quite an impracticable standard, I am advised by my chief analyst.

Was not the effect this, that the law provided that certain evidence shall be admissible? That was the evidence of a certain analyst, I do not know whether the chief analyst or not. That law was changed so as to enable the minister to select analysts all over, but when the certificate of any such inspector was taken into court it could not be accepted as evidence, because the Act provided that only the certificate of another analyst could be accepted, and that other analyst had never analysed the sample.

I would suggest that this amendment be added to clause 12:
All inspectors of fertilizers shall, whenever so instructed by the minister, obtain for analysis a sample of every fertilizer for sale in the district for which he is inspector, and shall forthwith lay the information and prosecute, in the event of the provisions of this Act not having been complied with.
The minister says that the chief analyst is the man who should prosecute. I wish to take issue with him. I know it is very difficult to get any authority away from the central department at Ottawa, but, as a matter of fact, the man who takes the sample from the parcel and sends it to the department in a registered letter, where it is analysed and a certificate given, is the man who should lay the information before a magistrate in his district. It is not the high court, I think, which deals with the matter. I make this suggestion because, under Acts of a similar character, for instance the Ontario License Act, the inspectors are the parties who prosecute and not the government. It is the duty of the officers, who are appointed to see that the law is carried out, to lay an information before a magistrate if they find that the law is broken.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I am afraid this would be delegating to officials of the government the authority to enteT prosecutions.	.
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: But all prosecutions are entered by the Justice Department. Speaking for the Inland Revenue Department, I am certain of that.
What about the Customs?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I am not sure.
Take the Marine Department; when there is a breach of the Marine Law, the inspector of hnlls may seize the vessel and prosecute the party.
Under the Fruit Marks Act, the local inspector has authority to lay the information.

It is always objectionable to make an inspector a prosecuting officer as well. There is a great difference between the customs officials and those under this Act. And the customs officers do not in all cases prosecute. They report to the department and get instructions. They cannot put the law in motion of their own free will. The hon. gentleman is mistaken about the license inspectors under the provincial law. They are not prosecuting officers or detectives in the sense he assumes. If a complaint is put into their hands they can act on it; in ordinary cases they act when they get their instructions.
Suppose an inland revenue inspector finds an illicit still?

If he is instructed to take action he does so; but an inland revenue officer, under provisions which might justify action regarding an illicit sale or manufacture of liquors, would be in a very different position from an officer under this Act taking the law into his own hands of his own sweet will. The people do not want to be dragooned in that way. It is bad legislation, and I do not think any member should propose it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: No doubt the officers of the Inland Revenue Department make seizures in the case of illicit distillation or for any infringement of the excise law, but every prosecution is made through the Justice Department.

I quite agree with the hon. minister, but the point I wish to make is this: somebody must lay the information, and the party who lays it is invariably the inspector. As Tegards the customs officers, the Customs Department is supreme in itself. There has been a clause in the Customs Act from time immemorial under which the Customs Department can seize an article and confiscate it and fine the guilty party. That department is above the Justice Department in that respect. Various attempts have been made in England to change that clause, but parliament would never grant authority to narrow down the powers of the Customs Department m that respect. An officer of the Inland Revenue Department can seize an article, and the department can impose a fine, and does not even have to take him before a magistrate.
Where does the hon. gentleman get that information?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The Inland Revenue Department does impose certain conditions.
If the party who has tried to defraud the revenue is willing to pay into the treasury a certain sum, he has the power to do so, but if he thinks that the department is trying to impose too onerous conditions, he can allow the matter to go to court, and then he is prosecuted by the Justice Department. If the department imposes a certain fine, he has the right to refuse to pay and to have his case heard in court.

One of the most satisfactory inspectorships we have in the province of Ontario is that of milk inspectors. They have power to inspect factories and to prosecute offenders. _ I do not think there has ever been an inspector in that province that has done so much good and has given the people so much satisfaction. But they are not responsible to the minister, nor to the government, nor to anybody, but their duties are defined by an Act of the legislature, and they are doing very effective work.

There must be somebody responsible to authorize the officer to
proceed.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: That somebody more responsible than the inspector is the Minister of Inland Revenue. The enforcement of the law is in the hands of the Minister of Inland Revenue.

I would like to see this Bill made workable. Let the minister suggest an amendment himself that would relieve him of responsibility. I think that if there were a great many requests coming in for prosecution, the minister would not feel so favourable to handing out his authorization. But if some inspector had the authority, it would relieve the minister, and the Act could be better enforced.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I have no objection to an amendment, say: ' And shall prosecute the offender whenever instructed by the minister to do so.'

I do not think that would make the law workable. What would be the result of that? The inspector knows that he has to make a report to the minister, that entails delay. Then he has to get instructions. Why, the whole position might be changed in the meantime, he might not be able to find the parties, and the whole conditions might be changed from what they weTe.

Where is the objection to empowering the inspector to prosecute under certain restrictions? If we pass an Act without providing any machinery to carry it out, what good will it do? There will have to be so many preliminaries before prosecutions can be undertaken that

the manufacturers will not fear the Act much. But if there is an inspector appointed, like the milk inspector in the province of Ontario, with power to prosecute for violations, I think the law would be much more workable.
There is great objection to giving power to a single individual to become a prosecuting officer on his own discretion. Such laws as that are of pretty ancient date, they have gone out of existence.
The liquor license inspectors have such power.

He can only prosecute under certain conditions. In the great majority of cases he makes his report to the government, and he is instructed to act! He has no more authority than a policeman, and a policeman can act in certain minor cases if he see the law being broken, but otherwise he has to get authority from a, magistrate to act under certain conditions. So it is with the license inspectors.

The hon. gentleman is entirely wrong as regards the province of Ontario. I know a case in my own county where the inspector goes to the hotel, and finding liquor there contrary to law, he seeks a magistrate, lays information and then proceeds with the charge.
This motion is to compel an officer to be prosecuting official. He has no choice, he would have no discretion in the matter.
The word is 'may' not ' shall.' It is not obligatory upon him.
Where the word 'may' is used that means ' shall ' in the law.

Under the Ontario Act no man other than the inspector has any thing to do with prosecutions. He lays the complaint and he prosecutes. I have been director of a cheese factory for many years, and I know how these cases are conducted. Under certain conditions the inspector is allowed to go on and prosecute, even without any preliminaries. In the present Act I would not put in a clause compelling him to go on, but I would provide that he shall have power to go on.
The milk inspector is an officer of the public health, and these officers have very wide powers. But a license inspector would not prosecute without referring the matter to his license board.
It is done every week m the year.
No. I have had some experience in this matter, and no license inspector would take action without reference to his commissioners.
I have seen it done more than once. The inspector goes into a place, finds a hotel violating the law, gives information, and lodges a complaint within two hours.
That is not my experience.
The methods in the small places and in the cities are evidently different.

I understood the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. J. A. Currie) to say that there are certain officers in the province of Ontario empowered to impose a fine without going to a magistrate. Is that what the hon. gentleman said?

No. The idea is to have somebody charged with the duty of conducting these prosecutions. If a farmer feels that he has been defrauded in a purchase of fertilizers, and, when he asks that a sample be taken and analysed, it is found that the material is wrong, the farmer who was the means of making known the case should not be called upon to lay the information against the storekeeper; outside officers should do that. I think the amendment proposed by the minister is acceptable.
If I understood the amendment, I object to it also.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
My hon. friend wants to give the inspectors power to prosecute, and I suggested that it should be under instructions by the minister. But, the amendment in that form would mean nothing, because in the case of a prosecution under this Act, the prosecutor is the minister, or the official of the department under the minister, which is the same thing. We may require our inspectors -under the Adulteration of Food Act or under this Act to prosecute offenders through the Justice Department,-all our legal business is done through the Justice Department.
On section 15-penalties-proviso as to evidence of fraudulent intent.
Does the minister intend to leave this only a money penalty? Is there to be no penalty in case of failure to pay the fine?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I should think the money penalty would be sufficient. However, I am in the judgment of the House on that matter.
Make it read that in default of payment of the fine the party should be imprisoned.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I am not averse to that if hon. members think it necessary.

The person prosecuted may be a man of straw, and it is better

that there should be something more than a money penalty.

I move that after the *words ' penalty not exceeding one hundred dollars ' the following words be added: ' and in default of payment of such fine to a term of imprisonment to one month in the common jail of the county or district where the prosection is laid.'
It is unnecessary to specify the place of imprisonment; that is provided for in the General Act.
Very well, leave that out.
It should be 'thirty days,' as ' one month ' is not a definite time.
There should be a discretion in the magistrate. It should read * not exceeding 30 days.'

I object to the very high price placed on that analysis, $5.
The resident agent is not made liable to the penalties under the Act. I would suggest a substantive clause making the resident agent of the foreign manufacturer liable for a breach of the Act.
Did the minister accept the suggestion of the reduction in the amount of the fee? I agree with the hon. member in that respect.

I would suggest to my hon. friend (Mr. S. Sharpe) that it would be better to make clause 4 at line 25 read: And such agent shall be subject to the same penalties and have the same responsibility as a manufacturer under the terms of this Act.
The minister said that any one who offered the article for sale would by that act become an agent, the vendor would become an agent.
I would think that in clause 15 'every person' includes the manufacturer and agent.
Under that provision the corner grocery man is responsible.
In the province of Quebec he would be responsible for the goods he sells.
Then the grocer will have to have an analysis of every sample he sells?

I would like to have a

agent.	.
I do not think you can makes a man responsible under the Code by inference.
I think the words mean he would really take the place in Canada of a manufacturer.
It would be better to have it clear as it is a penalty clause.

House in committee on Bill (No. 90) to create the Department of External Affairs. -Mr. Murphy.
1.	There shall be a department of the gov-ornment of Canada to be called the Department of External Affairs, over which the Secretary of State for the time being shall preside.
The words 'for the time being' might be omitted.
That section is exactly the same as the similar sections in the other statutes creating departments.
There seems to be a great diversity in the language of the sections creating the different departments, and one would think it desirable to have them as uniform as possible.
I do not see how we can have uniformity without recasting the other statutes.

The statute creating the department of Secretary of State uses these words:-'and the Secretary of State shall have the management and control of the department.' Was there any reason for omitting these words here.
No.

I wonder why the words were omitted, but it does not make much difference.
2.	The Governor in Council may appoint an officer who shall be called the Under 'Secretary of State for External Affairs, and who shall be the deputy head of the department, and may also appoint such other officers and c'erks as are requisite for the due administration of the business of the department, all of whom shall hold office during pleasure.
The section says that there shall be an under Secretary of State for External Affairs but there does not seem to be any Secretary of State for External Affairs.

The position would be analogous to the Interior Department and

the Department of Indian Affairs which are under one minister, and also the Labour Department and the Post Office Department which are in the same position.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: After private Bills, and motions, and questions we shall go into Committee of Supply so as to give an opportunity to the member for .North Toronto to bring up a certain matter of which he has given notice.

As I have mentioned to the Prime Minister privately, the hour may be so far advanced that the hon. member for North Toronto would not think it desirable to bring on his motion that day. That will depend on circumstances. He is absent at present but as soon as he returns from Toronto I will ascertain from him his views and communicate with the Prime Minister.
